Uniform in time L∞L^{\infty}-estimates for an attraction-repulsion chemotaxis model with double saturation

Abstract.

In this paper we focus on this attraction-repulsion chemotaxis model with consumed signals

(◇\Diamond) {ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)+ξ∇⋅(u∇w) in ​Ω×(0,Tm​a​x),vt=Δ​v−u​v in ​Ω×(0,Tm​a​x),wt=Δ​w−u​w in ​Ω×(0,Tm​a​x),\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+\xi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla w)&\text{ in }\Omega\times(0,T_{max}),\\ v_{t}=\Delta v-uv&\text{ in }\Omega\times(0,T_{max}),\\ w_{t}=\Delta w-uw&\text{ in }\Omega\times(0,T_{max}),\end{cases}

formulated in a bounded and smooth domain Ω\Omega of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, with n≥2n\geq 2, for some positive real numbers χ,ξ\chi,\xi and with Tm​a​x∈(0,∞]T_{max}\in(0,\infty]. Once equipped with appropriately smooth initial distributions u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x)≥0u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)\geq 0, v⁡(x,0)=v0​(x)≥0v(x,0)=v_{0}(x)\geq 0 and w⁡(x,0)=w0​(x)≥0w(x,0)=w_{0}(x)\geq 0, as well as Neumann boundary conditions, we establish sufficient assumptions on its data yielding global and bounded classical solutions; these are functions u,vu,v and ww, with zero normal derivative on ∂Ω×(0,Tm​a​x)\partial\Omega\times(0,T_{max}), satisfying pointwise the equations in problem ( ◇ ) with Tm​a​x=∞T_{max}=\infty. This is proved for any such initial data, whenever χ\chi and ξ\xi belong to bounded and open intervals, depending respectively on ‖v0‖L∞​(Ω)\|v_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)} and ‖w0‖L∞​(Ω)\|w_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}. Finally, we illustrate some aspects of the dynamics present within the chemotaxis system by means of numerical simulations.

Key words and phrases: 
Chemotaxis, Attraction-Repulsion, Global existence, Boundedness, Consumption.

1. Introduction, main claim and organization of the paper

1.1. The model: discussion and presentation of the main result

Since the advent in the 70’s of the biological Keller–Segel models ([10, 11, 12]) idealizing chemotaxis phenomena, many related variants have been finding interest in the mathematical community. Indeed, when facing such problems several technical difficulties appear; of course, this encourages and stimulates researchers in this field.

In this regard, the model inspiring this article can be formulated as:

(1) {ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)+ξ∇⋅(u∇w) in ​Ω×(0,Tm​a​x),τ​vt=Δ​v−β​v+h⁡(u,v) in ​Ω×(0,Tm​a​x),τ​wt=Δ​w−δ​w+k⁡(u,v) in ​Ω×(0,Tm​a​x),with{uν=vν=wν=0 on ​∂Ω×(0,Tm​a​x),u​(x,0)=u0​(x)x∈Ω¯,v​(x,0)=v0​(x)x∈Ω¯,w​(x,0)=w0​(x)x∈Ω¯.\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+\xi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla w)&\text{ in }\Omega\times(0,T_{max}),\\ \tau v_{t}=\Delta v-\beta v+h(u,v)&\text{ in }\Omega\times(0,T_{max}),\\ \tau w_{t}=\Delta w-\delta w+k(u,v)&\text{ in }\Omega\times(0,T_{max}),\end{cases}\quad\textrm{with}\quad\begin{cases}u_{\nu}=v_{\nu}=w_{\nu}=0&\text{ on }\partial\Omega\times(0,T_{max}),\\ u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)&x\in\bar{\Omega},\\ v(x,0)=v_{0}(x)&x\in\bar{\Omega},\\ w(x,0)=w_{0}(x)&x\in\bar{\Omega}.\end{cases}

Herein Ω\Omega is a bounded and smooth domain of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, with n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, τ∈{0,1}\tau\in\{0,1\}, χ,ξ,β,δ>0\chi,\xi,\beta,\delta>0 and h=h⁡(ξ,η)h=h(\xi,\eta) and k=k⁡(ξ,η)k=k(\xi,\eta) are some regular functions of their arguments ξ≥0\xi\geq 0 and η≥0\eta\geq 0. Moreover, further regular initial data u0​(x)≥0u_{0}(x)\geq 0, v0​(x)≥0v_{0}(x)\geq 0 and w0​(x)≥0w_{0}(x)\geq 0 are as well given, the subscript ν\nu in (⋅)ν(\cdot)_{\nu} indicates the outward normal derivative on ∂Ω\partial\Omega, whereas Tm​a​x∈(0,∞]T_{max}\in(0,\infty] the maximal time up to which solutions to the system are defined.

In order to properly interpret the mathematical formulation in (1) in the context of real biological phenomena, we specify the following: if u=u⁡(x,t)u=u(x,t) denotes a certain cell distribution (populations, organisms) at the position xx and at the time tt, and v=v⁡(x,t)v=v(x,t) and w=w⁡(x,t)w=w(x,t) stand for the concentrations of chemoattractant and chemorepellent (i.e. a chemical signal inducing the cells to, respectively, attract each other and repulse from the other), the system idealizes the motion of the cells, inside an insulated domain (zero-flux on the border: homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions) and initially distributed accordingly to the law of u0u_{0}. More precisely, such an evolution is influenced by the competition between the aggregation/repulsion impact (configured at the initial time conforming to v0v_{0} and w0w_{0}) from the cross terms χu∇v/ξu∇w\chi u\nabla v/\xi u\nabla w both increasing for larger sizes of χ\chi and ξ\xi and evolving also following the rates h⁡(u,v)h(u,v) and k⁡(u,v)k(u,v), respectively (second and third equations in (1)). To give an idea of its applicability in the real world, model (1) has been proposed to describe the aggregation of microglia involved in the inflammation observed in Alzheimer’s disease ([16]); herein, dimensional, numerical and experimental analyses, in one-dimensional settings, have been proposed for the fully parabolic version (i.e. τ=1\tau=1 in both equations) when h⁡(u,v)h(u,v) and k⁡(u,v)k(u,v) are linear functions only of the cell density (formulations of this type are also known as signal-production models).

The aforementioned interplay between the factors describing model (1) strongly influences the cellular motility: in particular, the evolution might relax toward global stabilization and convergence to equilibrium of the cell distribution uu, but could even degenerate into the so-called chemotactic collapse, the mechanism resulting in uncontrolled aggregation processes for uu, eventually blowing up/exploding at finite time. In particular, moving toward more purely mathematical interpretations (for which we are more interested herein), in the first case, solutions (u,v,w)(u,v,w) are defined and bounded for all (x,t)(x,t) in Ω×(0,∞)\Omega\times(0,\infty), in the other, for a certain finite time Tm​a​xT_{max}, the solution (u,v,w)(u,v,w) ceases to exist for larger value of Tm​a​xT_{max} and becomes unbounded approaching Tm​a​xT_{max}. Wanting to provide some details in this framework, for the fully elliptic version (i.e. τ=0\tau=0 in the equations for vv and ww) of model (1) these results are available in the literature. When linear growths of the chemoattractant and the chemorepellent are considered, h⁡(u,v)=α​uh(u,v)=\alpha u, α>0\alpha>0, and k⁡(u,v)=γ​uk(u,v)=\gamma u, γ>0\gamma>0, the value ξ​γ−χ​α\xi\gamma-\chi\alpha, measuring the difference between the repulsion and attraction contributions, is critical for n=2n=2: particularly, if ξ​γ−χ​α>0\xi\gamma-\chi\alpha>0 (repulsion dominated regime), in any dimension all solutions to the model are globally bounded, whereas for ξ​γ−χ​α<0\xi\gamma-\chi\alpha<0 (attraction dominated regime) unbounded solutions can be detected (see [7, 15, 24, 25, 32] for some connected studies). On the other hand, for more general production laws, respectively hh and kk generalizing the prototypes h⁡(u,v)=α​ush(u,v)=\alpha u^{s}, s>0,s>0, and k⁡(u,v)=γ​urk(u,v)=\gamma u^{r}, r≥1r\geq 1, we are only aware of the following recent result, valid for n≥2n\geq 2 ([26]): for every α,β,γ,δ,χ>0\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta,\chi>0, and r>s≥1r>s\geq 1 (resp. s>r≥1s>r\geq 1), there exists ξ∗>0\xi^{*}>0 (resp. ξ∗>0\xi_{*}>0) such that if ξ>ξ∗\xi>\xi^{*} (resp. ξ≥ξ∗\xi\geq\xi_{*}), any sufficiently regular initial distribution u0​(x)≥0u_{0}(x)\geq 0 (resp. u0​(x)≥0u_{0}(x)\geq 0 enjoying some smallness assumptions) infers a unique classical and bounded solution. In addition the same conclusion holds true for every α,β,γ,δ,χ,ξ>0\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta,\chi,\xi>0, 0<s<10<s<1, r=1r=1 and any sufficiently regular u0​(x)≥0u_{0}(x)\geq 0.

The chemotactic collapse discussed for the signal-production model (1) is a scenario difficult to detect for alike signal-absorption models. Indeed, even for the original Keller–Segel system with consumption

(2) {ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v) in ​Ω×(0,Tm​a​x),vt=Δ​v−u​v in ​Ω×(0,Tm​a​x),with{uν=vν=0 on ​∂Ω×(0,Tm​a​x),u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x),v⁡(x,0)=v0​(x)x∈Ω¯,\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)&\text{ in }\Omega\times(0,T_{max}),\\ v_{t}=\Delta v-uv&\text{ in }\Omega\times(0,T_{max}),\end{cases}\quad\textrm{with}\quad\begin{cases}u_{\nu}=v_{\nu}=0&\text{ on }\partial\Omega\times(0,T_{max}),\\ u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),\;v(x,0)=v_{0}(x)&\;x\in\bar{\Omega},\end{cases}

and corresponding to the simplified two-unknowns version of problem (1) whit h⁡(u,v)=β​v−u​vh(u,v)=\beta v-uv, the occurrence of blow-up has not been found yet. This is also connected to the observation that comparison arguments suddenly imply (from the second equation) that the chemical distribution vv, responsible for gathering phenomena, is uniformly bounded. Despite that, such a bound by itself is not enough to ensure that classical solutions (u,v)(u,v) to (2) emanating from any sufficiently regular initial data (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}) are also uniformly bounded. Precisely, this holds true only in two-dimensional settings: this is achieved in [30] and [31], where for a more general coupled chemotaxis-fluid model, respectively globality and convergence of classical solutions are derived. Conversely, in [23] it is established that for n≥3n\geq 3 the smallness assumption χ∥v0∥L∞​(Ω)≤16​(n+1)\chi\lVert v_{0}\lVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq\frac{1}{6(n+1)} is required. (This condition has then been improved in χ∥v0∥L∞​(Ω)<π2​(n+1)\chi\lVert v_{0}\lVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}<\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2(n+1)}}; see [2].) In particular, attempts to ensure boundedness of solutions to variants tied to problem (2) even when χ∥v0∥L∞​(Ω)\chi\lVert v_{0}\lVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)} is larger than 16​(n+1)\frac{1}{6(n+1)} (or π2​(n+1)\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2(n+1)}}) have been proposed; we here mention the following two results. In [14], where logistic sources with strong damping effects in the equation of the cells have been introduced, reading

ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)+ku−μu2, in Ω×(0,Tm​a​x),k,μ>0,u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+ku-\mu u^{2},\quad\text{ in }\Omega\times(0,T_{max}),\quad k,\mu>0,

the authors establish that the resulting Cauchy problem admits classical bounded solutions for arbitrarily large χ∥v0∥L∞​(Ω)\chi\lVert v_{0}\lVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)} provided μ\mu is also larger than a certain expression increasing with χ∥v0∥L∞​(Ω)\chi\lVert v_{0}\lVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}. But, going towards attraction-repulsion models, when in (1) one considers h⁡(u,v)≈β​v−uα​vh(u,v)\approx\beta v-u^{\alpha}v in the second equation (with τ=1\tau=1) and k⁡(u,v)≈ulk(u,v)\approx u^{l} in the third (with τ=0\tau=0), a model with produced chemorepellent and saturated chemoattractant is obtained; in [6] boundedness is proved (i) for l=1l=1, n∈{1,2}n\in\{1,2\}, α∈(0,12+1n)∩(0,1)\alpha\in(0,\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{n})\cap(0,1) and any ξ>0\xi>0, (ii) for l=1l=1, n≥3n\geq 3, α∈(0,12+1n)\alpha\in(0,\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{n}) and ξ\xi larger than a quantity depending on χ​∥v0∥L∞​(Ω)\chi\lVert v_{0}\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}, (iii) for l>1l>1 any ξ>0\xi>0, and in any dimensional settings. (Even though herein we are not strictly interested in the influence of logistics in chemotaxis models, we discussed its role in connection to problems of the form in (2). Henceforth, we believe that the same is worthwhile to do for formulations quite close to (1); see, for instance to [18, 19, 20].)

Exactly with the purpose of investigating more deeply the repulsion effect in chemotaxis models like (1), we therein fix h⁡(u,v)=β​v−u​vh(u,v)=\beta v-uv and h⁡(u,v)=δ​w−u​wh(u,v)=\delta w-uw, thus arriving at this attraction-repulsion system with double saturation:

(3) {ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)+ξ∇⋅(u∇w) in ​Ω×(0,Tm​a​x),vt=Δ​v−u​v in ​Ω×(0,Tm​a​x),wt=Δ​w−u​w in ​Ω×(0,Tm​a​x),uν=vν=wν=0 on ​∂Ω×(0,Tm​a​x),u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x),v⁡(x,0)=v0​(x),w⁡(x,0)=w0​(x)x∈Ω¯.\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+\xi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla w)&\text{ in }\Omega\times(0,T_{max}),\\ v_{t}=\Delta v-uv&\text{ in }\Omega\times(0,T_{max}),\\ w_{t}=\Delta w-uw&\text{ in }\Omega\times(0,T_{max}),\\ u_{\nu}=v_{\nu}=w_{\nu}=0&\text{ on }\partial\Omega\times(0,T_{max}),\\ u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),\;v(x,0)=v_{0}(x),\;w(x,0)=w_{0}(x)&x\in\bar{\Omega}.\end{cases}

Considering what has been said before, this problem is a natural completion of the above studies on the attraction-repulsion models with only production and with production and consumption.

As far as we know, a general nn-dimensional theoretical analysis tied to the Cauchy boundary problem (3) has not been developed yet; hereafter, we aim at providing some partial results to extend the corresponding mathematical comprehension. Specifically, we will derive sufficient conditions involving the data of the model such that the actions of the consumed chemoattractant and chemorepellent guarantee its well-posedness. More precisely, we shall prove this

Theorem 1.1.

For any n≥2n\geq 2 and some r>nr>n, let Ω\Omega be a smooth and bounded domain of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} and (u0,v0,w0)∈(W1,r​(Ω))3(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0})\in(W^{1,r}(\Omega))^{3} any nontrivial initial data with u0,v0,w0≥0u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}\geq 0 on Ω¯\bar{\Omega}. Then, for 0<χ<15​n​‖v0‖L∞​(Ω)0<\chi<\frac{1}{5n\|v_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}} and 0<ξ<15​n​‖w0‖L∞​(Ω)0<\xi<\frac{1}{5n\|w_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}} there exists a unique triplet of nonnegative functions

(u,v,w)∈(C0​([0,∞),W1,r​(Ω))∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(0,∞)))3(u,v,w)\in(C^{0}([0,\infty);W^{1,r}(\Omega))\cap C^{2,1}(\bar{\Omega}\times(0,\infty)))^{3}

solving problem (3) and uniformly bounded in time.

1.2. Technical strategy and structure of the article

In our work we will adapt mathematical reasoning given in [23], and referred to the above introduced consumption chemotaxis model with only attraction. In both cases, the related steps toward boundedness are connected to some a priori estimates of ∫Ωuk=∫Ωuk​(x,t)​𝑑x\int_{\Omega}u^{k}=\int_{\Omega}u^{k}(x,t)dx, for some k>1k>1 and some t>0t>0, with uu being any given solution to problem (3) or (2). In this direction, by using boundedness of vv and ww or vv (automatically coming from the parabolic maximum principle), we can face each problem by suitably employing functionals of the form ∫Ωuk​φ\int_{\Omega}u^{k}\varphi. Herein, φ\varphi is an ad hoc function, positive and bounded together with its derivatives; it, consistently with the investigated model, moreover depends on (v,w)(v,w) or vv. Indeed, an evolutive analysis of such a functional leads to a crucial absorption differential inequality in time for the functional itself, and in turn to the desired bound for ∫Ωuk\int_{\Omega}u^{k}. It should be noticed that, evidently, further technical difficulties appear when controlling dd​t​∫Ωuk​φ\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}u^{k}\varphi associated to problem (3); in fact it has one more unknown than (2).

The rest of the paper is structured as follows. First, in §\lx@sectionsign2 we prove the local existence and uniqueness of a classical solution to model (3) and some of its properties. In this same section we give a criterion establishing how to ensure globability and boundedness of local solutions using some of their a priori LpL^{p}-boundedness. In turn, §\lx@sectionsign3 is exactly devoted to the derivation of these bounds, by means of which we can deduce the proof of Theorem 1.1. Finally, we present some discussions in §\lx@sectionsign4 and, moreover, the theoretical results presented here are investigated numerically in §\lx@sectionsign5, where two- and three-dimensional simulations are used to discuss how parameters involved in (2) and (3) influence the behaviors of their solutions.

2. Existence of local-in-time solutions and main properties

In order to address questions tied to existence and properties of solutions to problem (3), let us write it in a more suitable form. Specifically, for ω=(ω1,ω2,ω3)=(u,v,w)\omega=(\omega_{1},\omega_{2},\omega_{3})=(u,v,w) and ω⁡(⋅,0)=(ω1,0,ω2,0,ω3,0)=(u0,v0,w0)\omega(\cdot,0)=(\omega_{1,0},\omega_{2,0},\omega_{3,0})=(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}), it can be rephrased as

(4) {ωt=∇⋅(𝒜(ω)∇ω)+ℱ(ω) in ​Ω×(0,Tm​a​x),ων=0 on ​∂Ω×(0,Tm​a​x),ω⁡(x,0)=(u0,v0,w0)x∈Ω¯,\begin{cases}\omega_{t}=\nabla\cdot(\mathcal{A}(\omega)\nabla\omega)+\mathcal{F}(\omega)&\text{ in }\Omega\times(0,T_{max}),\\ \omega_{\nu}=0&\text{ on }\partial\Omega\times(0,T_{max}),\\ \omega(x,0)=(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0})&x\in\bar{\Omega},\end{cases}

where

𝒜⁡(ω)=(𝒜11​(ω)𝒜12​(ω)𝒜13​(ω)𝒜21​(ω)𝒜22​(ω)𝒜23​(ω)𝒜31​(ω)𝒜32​(ω)𝒜33​(ω))=(1−χ​uξ​u010001)and ℱ⁡(ω)=(ℱ1​(ω)ℱ2​(ω)ℱ3​(ω))=(0−u​v−u​w).\mathcal{A}(\omega)=\begin{pmatrix}\mathcal{A}_{11}(\omega)&\mathcal{A}_{12}(\omega)&\mathcal{A}_{13}(\omega)\\ \mathcal{A}_{21}(\omega)&\mathcal{A}_{22}(\omega)&\mathcal{A}_{23}(\omega)\\ \mathcal{A}_{31}(\omega)&\mathcal{A}_{32}(\omega)&\mathcal{A}_{33}(\omega)\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-\chi u&\xi u\\ 0&1&0\\ 0&0&1\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{and }\quad\mathcal{F}(\omega)=\begin{pmatrix}\mathcal{F}_{1}(\omega)\\ \mathcal{F}_{2}(\omega)\\ \mathcal{F}_{3}(\omega)\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\ -uv\\ -uw\end{pmatrix}.

With these preparations in our hands, we give the following

Definition 2.1.

For any n≥2n\geq 2, some r>nr>n and T>0T>0, let Ω\Omega be a smooth and bounded domain of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} and (u0,v0,w0)∈(W1,r​(Ω))3(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0})\in(W^{1,r}(\Omega))^{3}. We say that ω∈(C⁡([0,T),W1,r​(Ω)))3\omega\in(C([0,T);W^{1,r}(\Omega)))^{3} is a weak W1,rW^{1,r}-solution of problem (4) in Ω×(0,T)\Omega\times(0,T), if for all test function φ∈C0∞​(Ω×[0,T))\varphi\in C_{0}^{\infty}(\Omega\times[0,T)) we have that for I,J,K=1,2,3I,J,K=1,2,3, with I≠J≠KI\neq J\neq K,

−∫0T∫ΩωIφt−∫ΩωI,0φ(⋅,0)=−∫0T∫Ω(𝒜I​I(ω)∇ωI+𝒜I​J(ω)∇ωJ+𝒜I​K(ω)∇ωK)⋅∇φ+∫0T∫ΩℱI(ω)φ.-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}\omega_{I}\varphi_{t}-\int_{\Omega}\omega_{I,0}\varphi(\cdot,0)=-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}(\mathcal{A}_{II}(\omega)\nabla\omega_{I}+\mathcal{A}_{IJ}(\omega)\nabla\omega_{J}+\mathcal{A}_{IK}(\omega)\nabla\omega_{K})\cdot\nabla\varphi+\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}\mathcal{F}_{I}(\omega)\varphi.

The forthcoming result ensures that Definition 2.1 is appropriate in terms of solvability of problem (3); indeed, it admits weak solutions which are at least local and actually classical. Moreover, they satisfy some uniform bounds.

Lemma 2.2 (Local existence).

For any n≥2n\geq 2 and some r>nr>n, let Ω\Omega be a smooth and bounded domain of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} and (u0,v0,w0)∈(W1,r​(Ω))3(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0})\in(W^{1,r}(\Omega))^{3} any nontrivial initial data with u0,v0,w0≥0u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}\geq 0 on Ω¯\bar{\Omega}. Then there exists Tm​a​x∈(0,∞]T_{max}\in(0,\infty] such that problem (3) admits a unique nonnegative local-in-time classical solution

(u,v,w)∈(C⁡([0,Tm​a​x),W1,r​(Ω))∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(0,Tm​a​x)))3.(u,v,w)\in(C([0,T_{max});W^{1,r}(\Omega))\cap C^{2,1}(\bar{\Omega}\times(0,T_{max})))^{3}.

In addition, the uu-component satisfies the mass conservation property, i.e.

(5) ∫Ωu⁡(x,t)​𝑑x=∫Ωu0​(x)​𝑑x=m>0for all ​t∈(0,Tm​a​x),\int_{\Omega}u(x,t)dx=\int_{\Omega}u_{0}(x)dx=m>0\quad\textrm{for all }\,t\in(0,T_{max}),

whilst the components vv and ww are such that

(6) 0≤v≤∥v0∥L∞​(Ω)and0≤w≤∥w0∥L∞​(Ω)inΩ×(0,Tm​a​x).0\leq v\leq\lVert v_{0}\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\quad\textrm{and}\quad 0\leq w\leq\lVert w_{0}\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\quad\textrm{in}\quad\Omega\times(0,T_{max}).

Moreover, if there exists some positive constant CC such that

(7) ‖(u⁡(⋅,t),v⁡(⋅,t),w⁡(⋅,t))‖L∞​(Ω)≤Cfor all ​0<t<Tm​a​x,\|(u(\cdot,t),v(\cdot,t),w(\cdot,t))\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq C\quad\text{for all }0<t<T_{max},

then Tm​a​x=∞T_{max}=\infty, and u,vu,v and ww are uniformly bounded.

Proof.

From the equivalence of the two problems (3) and (4), the existence of a unique maximal weak W1,rW^{1,r}-solution, in the sense of Definition 2.1 and defined in (0,Tm​a​x)(0,T_{max}), is consequence of [1, Theorem 14.4]. In turn, [1, Theorem 14.6] ensures that such a solution is classical. As to its global boundedness, whenever criterion (7) is fulfilled, this is deduced by invoking [1, Theorem 15.5]. In addition, since ℱ1​(0,ω2,ω3)=0\mathcal{F}_{1}(0,\omega_{2},\omega_{3})=0, u¯≡0\underline{u}\equiv 0 is a sub-solution of the first equation in (3), so that from u0≥0u_{0}\geq 0 the uu-component is a super-solution and hence the parabolic maximum principle implies u≥u¯≡0u\geq\underline{u}\equiv 0 in Ω×(0,Tm​a​x)\Omega\times(0,T_{max}). Similar arguments provide the bounds in (6). Finally the mass conservation property follows by integrating over Ω\Omega the first equation of (3), in conjunction with the boundary conditions and the initial data u0​(x)u_{0}(x). ∎

As it is well known, once local solutions (u,v,w)(u,v,w) are given, they are globally bounded if some uniform in time estimate of their components in proper Sobolev spaces Wk,q​(Ω)W^{k,q}(\Omega) can be achieved. Herein, we present for convenience some steps showing that boundedness is implied whenever u∈L∞​((0,Tm​a​x),Lk​(Ω))u\in L^{\infty}((0,T_{max});L^{k}(\Omega)) for kk larger but arbitrarily close to n2\frac{n}{2}; details and generalizations are available in [3, 9, 29].

Lemma 2.3.

Under the hypotheses of Lemma 2.2, let (u,v,w)(u,v,w) be such that for some k>n2k>\frac{n}{2} the uu-component belongs to L∞​((0,Tm​a​x),Lk​(Ω))L^{\infty}((0,T_{max});L^{k}(\Omega)). Then u,vu,v and ww are uniformly bounded in time.

4. On the use of the functional ∫Ωuk​φ​(v,w)\int_{\Omega}u^{k}\varphi(v,w): miscellaneous

The closing part of the paper is concerned with the efficacy of the functional ∫Ωuk​φ​(v,w)\int_{\Omega}u^{k}\varphi(v,w) toward the derivation of the described results. In this regard we understand that the following comments worth to be analyzed.

4.1. Improving the condition in [23, Theorem 1.1]

The condition 0<χ≤16​(n+1)​‖v0‖L∞​(Ω)0<\chi\leq\frac{1}{6(n+1)\|v_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}} in [23], related to the consumption model with only attractive chemical signal, can be improved to 0<χ<23​n​‖v0‖L∞​(Ω)0<\chi<\frac{2}{3n\|v_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}}. 4.2. The attraction model vs. the attraction-repulsion model

In connection with what we have now done, let us attempt to compare the consumption model with only attraction and its counterpart complemented also with repulsive effects, that is the two models below

𝒫χ:{ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v),vt=Δ​v−u​v,and𝒫χ,ξ:{ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)+ξ∇⋅(u∇w),vt=Δ​v−u​v,wt=Δ​w−u​w,with{boundary conditions,initial conditions.\mathcal{P}_{\chi}:\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v),\\ v_{t}=\Delta v-uv,\end{cases}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal{P}_{\chi,\xi}:\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+\xi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla w),\\ v_{t}=\Delta v-uv,\\ w_{t}=\Delta w-uw,\end{cases}\quad\text{with}\quad\begin{cases}\textrm{boundary conditions},\\ \textrm{initial conditions}.\end{cases}

Using the same notation employed to define the interval in (20), let ℐχ,ξ\mathcal{I}_{\chi,\xi} be the interval of χ\chi where boundedness of solutions to problem 𝒫χ,ξ\mathcal{P}_{\chi,\xi} may be ensured; ℐχ\mathcal{I}_{\chi}, naturally, stands for that related to problem 𝒫χ\mathcal{P}_{\chi}. Even though by biological intuitions it should be conceivable that ℐχ,ξ⊃ℐχ\mathcal{I}_{\chi,\xi}\supset\mathcal{I}_{\chi} for every ξ>0\xi>0, this cannot be directly deduced by employing the functionals ∫Ωuk​φ\int_{\Omega}u^{k}\varphi. Indeed, by observing from (11) that taking (ϵ3,ϵ4)→(0,0)(\epsilon_{3},\epsilon_{4})\to(0,0) and (ϵ1,ϵ2)→(k−12,1χ)(\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2})\to\left(\sqrt{\frac{k-1}{2}},\sqrt{\frac{1}{\chi}}\right) corresponds to reduce/increase as much as possible the repulsion/attraction strength, the conclusion of Theorem 1.1 would apply for positive ξ\xi arbitrarily small, and χ\chi positive up (depending on ξ\xi) to the supremum value 25​n​∥v0∥L∞​(Ω)\frac{2}{5n\lVert v_{0}\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}}. Nevertheless, the resulting limit interval (0,25​n​∥v0∥L∞​(Ω))\left(0,\frac{2}{5n\lVert v_{0}\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}}\right) would remain strictly included in ℐχ\mathcal{I}_{\chi}. We understand that the reason of this undesired outcome is connected to the quantity of terms inherited from the functional in terms of the unknowns and equations of the problem: two in 𝒫χ\mathcal{P}_{\chi}, three in 𝒫χ,ξ\mathcal{P}_{\chi,\xi}. As analyzed, the exceeding part from the larger system produces extra addends implying that certain conclusions hold true for ranges of χ\chi smaller than those linked to the other system. However, aided by the next simulations, and in particular those explained in §\lx@sectionsign5.3, we can conclude that the aforementioned intuition is rather founded.

5. Numerical simulations

In this section we numerically test the presented theoretical results by simulating systems (2) and (3) in two and three dimensions (also abbreviated with 2​d2d and 3​d3d). Our computational and quantitative experiments are meant to support and complement the qualitative analyses in the earlier sections.

5.1. Methodology, difficulties and computational devices

Numerical simulations of chemotaxis-type systems, like those now mentioned, are by no means an easy goal but, on the contrary, a challenging task. Indeed, the solutions to such systems may exhibit interesting mathematical properties which cannot be easily reproduced in a discrete framework. In particular, it is rather difficult to develop numerical schemes preserving desired properties of solutions, like non-negativity or energy laws; moreover, it is also far from being a standard task capturing possible blow-up phenomena. (Some hints describing the technical details behind this complexity may be found, for instance, in [4, 33, 21, 8, 5].)

In our forthcoming 2​d2d/3​d3d simulations for both models (3) and (2), we introduce a Finite Element Method (FEM) space discretization, defined on a triangular/tetrahedral mesh with size hh of the domain Ω\Omega, with first order piecewise polynomials. On the other hand, we consider an implicit Euler scheme for the time discretization Δ​t\Delta t, where each time step is split into two stages. First we compute vv and ww as solutions of the (uncoupled) linear parabolic equations modeling the consumption, being uu explicitly known from the previous time step. Then the values of uu at any node of the mesh are updated by solving the chemotaxis equation, exactly using the gained quantities of the attraction and repulsion terms vv and ww at those nodes. (We specify that for the computation we used the open source library FEniCS ([13]) and a parallel solver has been employed at each time step for the resolution of the FEM linear systems.) It is precisely in this latter chemotaxis stage where the more severe difficulties arise. In fact, the numerical treatment of the taxis-driven terms may conduce to undesirable effects (especially in three-dimensional settings), as the mentioned loss of positivity of uu and/or related spurious oscillations, with consequent disastrous results. However, the combination of the Flux-Corrected Transport technique ([22]) and the use of proper devices (in the specific, a computer with two processors AMD Opteron 6320, 32 cores and 1Tb of RAM) allow us to circumvent these situations, hence achieving qualitatively acceptable results.

5.2. Simulations of model (2)

Through the following simulations, we essentially aim at corroborating the absence of blow-up solutions to the classical consumption model even for large values of the chemoattractant χ\chi associated to the attractive chemical agent vv.

5.2.1. Two-dimensional numerical tests.

The first test focuses on the two-dimensional case for the classical consumption model (2). We consider a mesh of the unit circle Ω={(x1,x2)∈ℝ2∣x12+x22<1}\Omega=\{(x_{1},x_{2})\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\,\mid\,x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}<1\}, meshed by 84673 triangular elements, with size h≃0.015h\simeq 0.015, and a time discretization Δ​t=0.00001\Delta t=0.00001. We take χ=20\chi=20 and the Gaussian bell-shaped initial values

u0​(x1,x2)=v0​(x1,x2)=20​e−30​(x12+x22).u_{0}(x_{1},x_{2})=v_{0}(x_{1},x_{2})=20\,e^{-30(x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2})}.

As said, the theory predicts that no blow-up occurs in the 2​d2d case; thereafter, this result may be employed to verify the consistency of our program. Indeed, in Figure 1 one can see that the attraction of vv leads to a growth of uu, which reaches its maximum value at t=0.0001t=0.0001. Then, due to the consumption effect from the second equation of  (2), big values of uu imply a reduction of those of vv and of ∇v\nabla v. This ends up allowing uu to decrease, due to the diffusive term. This can be clearly seen again in Figure 1, where the maximum of uu decreases and a plateau is produced at t=0.0010t=0.0010. The decrease of vv and of its gradient becomes more evident for higher values of time.

5.2.2. Three-dimensional numerical tests.

Once our program is validated in a two-dimensional domain, we apply it in 3​d3d, where some theoretical aspects remain without a response and have to be still investigated. It is worthwhile to emphasize that even though three-dimensional simulations were highly demanding from a computational point of view, the results shown below are quite satisfactory and support our methodology. We repeat the same test described in §\lx@sectionsign5.2.1, but on a unit sphere Ω={(x1,x2,x3)∈ℝ3∣x12+x22+x32<1}\Omega=\{(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})\in\mathbb{R}^{3}\,\mid\,x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+x_{3}^{2}<1\}, whose mesh is composed by 159296159296 elements (tetrahedrons) with maximum size h≃0.11h\simeq 0.11. We take as initial data

(21) u0(x1,x2,x3)=v0(x1,x2,x3)=20e−30​(x12+x22+x32).u_{0}(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})=v_{0}(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})=20\,e^{-30\*(x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+x_{3}^{2})}.

Moreover, being ∥v0∥L∞​(Ω)=20\lVert v_{0}\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}=20, we also fix χ=20≫0.055536≃π20​8\chi=20\gg 0.055536\simeq\frac{\pi}{20\sqrt{8}} (recall the condition for global boundedness χ​∥v0∥L∞​(Ω)<π2​(n+1)\chi\lVert v_{0}\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}<\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2(n+1)}} discussed in §\lx@sectionsign1.1). In this case, we have no theoretical result confirming or denying existence of unbounded solutions, but the simulations do not succumb to blow-up phenomena for model (2) nor in 3​d3d. Specifically, the results are qualitatively similar to the two-dimensional ones. As a matter of fact, as contextualized in Figure 2, the initial cells’ density grows until reaching its maximum value at t=0.005t=0.005; then, as the consumption effect weakens the attractive action of the chemical vv, further growth is prevented and uu decreases (invalidating a possible blow-up mechanism), as specially shown at t=0.01t=0.01 and t=0.05t=0.05.

5.2.3. Two- and three-dimensional numerical tests.

Figure 3 indicates that in two-dimensional settings, the cells’ distribution initially suffers a stronger spike than that detected in 3​d3d; in particular the maximum of uu in 2​d2d is reached earlier than in 3​d3d. This appears consistent with the behavior of chemical agent vv, whose maximum at the beginning is higher in 3​d3d. On the other hand, for the same dynamics, the maximum value of uu is achieved in the three-dimensional scenario; this is consistent with the well known phenomenon according to which in high dimensions blow-up phenomena in chemotaxis models are more conceivable than in lower dimensions. Additionally, when time increases, constant steady states for uu and vv (data not shown for the chemical) are achieved.

5.3. Simulations of model (3)

Through the following simulations, we essentially aim at showing that the introduction in the classical consumption mechanism of a further absorbed repulsive-chemical signal ww, enforces smoothness of solutions to the model even for large values of the chemoattractant χ\chi, associated to vv, and a small chemorepellent ξ\xi, connected to ww.

5.3.1. Two- and three-dimensional numerical tests.

In this section we discuss behaviors of the solution to system (3) in the two- and three-dimensional cases. Once the value of ξ>0\xi>0 is fixed, the remaining data used in these tests are the same than those employed in §\lx@sectionsign5.2.1, and precisely χ=20\chi=20 and u0​(x1,x2,x3)=v0​(x1,x2,x3)=w0​(x1,x2,x3)u_{0}(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})=v_{0}(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})=w_{0}(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}) as in expression (21). In this sense, Figure 4 allows us to discuss the evolution of the maximum of uu for different values of the parameter ξ\xi. (Note that as much χ=20\chi=20 as well as any value of ξ\xi sensitively surpass the quantity 0.0033≃115⋅200.0033\simeq\frac{1}{15\cdot 20}, computed according to the assumptions in Theorem 1.1.) As expected, a simple parameter sweep shows that the maximum of uu is higher/lower when ξ\xi is small/large. Nevertheless, this one-to-one correspondence occurs only at the beginning and at the end of the simulations; for intermediate time steps, the curves drawing the maximum of uu intersect each other without any clear pattern. In particular, for (the limit case) ξ=0\xi=0 no repulsion effect on the cells’ motion takes part on the dynamics, and the most pronounced spike is produced. Conversely, when ξ=χ=20\xi=\chi=20, attraction and repulsion symmetrically counteract each other, so that the only appreciated effect is reduced to the pure diffusion of living cells, with no chemotaxis phenomenon.
